source.title: US History Ch. 21: The Civil Rights Movement, 1954–1968

concepts.name: Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state what Brown decided and why it mattered as a starting point.

concepts.name: Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can trace the boycott from Parks's arrest to the court ruling and explain what it demonstrated.

concepts.name: Little Rock Nine (1957)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain why Little Rock showed that court rulings needed federal enforcement.

concepts.name: Greensboro sit-ins (1960)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain how the sit-ins worked as nonviolent direct action and what organization grew from them.

concepts.name: Freedom Rides (1961)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain what the Freedom Rides tested and how violence produced federal action.

concepts.name: Birmingham campaign (1963)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can connect the Birmingham images to the proposal of the Civil Rights Act.

concepts.name: March on Washington (1963)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state the march's goals and its role in building support for the bill.

concepts.name: Civil Rights Act of 1964
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state what the 1964 act banned and distinguish it from the 1965 act.

concepts.name: Selma and the Voting Rights Act (1965)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can connect Selma to the Voting Rights Act and state what the act did.

concepts.name: Primary vs. secondary sources
concepts.learningObjective: The student can classify a document as primary or secondary from who made it, when, and why.

concepts.name: Cause and effect in the movement
concepts.learningObjective: The student can chain at least four events of the movement from cause to consequence.

title: The Civil Rights Files

theme.setting: A newspaper archive whose files walk you from 1954 to 1965
theme.tone: noir, investigative, respectful of the people in the story

premise: The paper locked its civil rights files. Walk the years from 1954 to 1965 and put the true story back.

characters.name: Ida the Archivist
characters.role: keeper of the files and your guide

characters.name: The Editor
characters.role: the voice locked in the last vault

encounters.prompt: Brown v. Board was a 1954 case about segregation, keeping Black and white students apart. Find the one false label.

statements.text: In 1954, the Court ruled that segregated schools can never be equal
Within a year, schools across the South let Black and white students learn together
statements.explanation: Many states fought it for years. Little Rock needed federal troops in 1957.

statements.text: The ruling threw out the old 'separate but equal' rule for schools
statements.explanation: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) said separate places were fine if they were 'equal.'

hints: The ruling came in 1954. Ask what schools really looked like in the years right after that.
Check each label against Little Rock in 1957. Nine students there needed soldiers to get into school.
The label about Plessy and 'separate but equal' is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That label is true. Look for the one about what schools did after the ruling.
encounters.debriefLine: The false label said "Within a year, schools across the South let Black and white students learn together." Brown came in 1954, but it took years and federal troops to change schools.

sourceRef.quote: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

encounters.targetMisconception: Rosa Parks was just a tired seamstress who acted alone.
encounters.prompt: In a boycott, people refuse to use something as a protest. Put the Montgomery bus boycott in order and skip the plank that never happened.

steps: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat and is arrested, December 1, 1955
Local leaders plan a one-day boycott, and it grows into a year-long one
Black riders in Montgomery stay off the buses for 381 days
The Supreme Court says bus segregation breaks the Constitution, and the boycott ends
decoys: Parks decides on the spot to start a protest movement all by herself

hints: Start with the arrest on December 1, 1955. Everything else grew out of that day.
Nobody walks for 381 days without a plan. Ask what had to happen before the long walk.
The plank about Parks acting all alone never happened. She was part of a group ready to act.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The boycott had to be planned before it could last 381 days. The court ruling came last.
encounters.debriefLine: You put the Montgomery boycott's 4 steps in order. One arrest grew into 381 days of planned protest that ended with a court win.

sourceRef.quote: The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after the Supreme Court affirmed that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

encounters.targetMisconception: Southern states complied with Brown once it was decided.
encounters.prompt: In September 1957, Arkansas's governor used the state's National Guard to block nine Black students from Central High. What does President Eisenhower do?

params.scenario: A federal court said the nine students could attend Central High. Governor Faubus used the state's National Guard to block them anyway.

options.text: Sends the 101st Airborne, an Army unit, to walk the students into school
options.explanation: Eisenhower took control of the Guard and sent Army troops to carry out the court order.

options.text: Lets Arkansas decide, since schools are a state matter
options.explanation: A state was ignoring a federal court order. The president stepped in to enforce it.

options.text: Cancels the school order to calm things down
options.explanation: The order stayed. The students went in with soldiers guarding them.

params.reveal: On September 25, 1957, soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division walked the nine students into Central High School.

hints: The governor is ignoring an order from a federal court. That's the fight here.
Ask who has more power than a governor when a federal court is ignored. Check each choice against that.
Canceling the order would mean the governor won. That's not what happened, so compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Brown didn't enforce itself. When a state ignored a federal court, it took the president and the Army.
encounters.debriefLine: At Little Rock, the answer was "Sends the 101st Airborne, an Army unit, to walk the students into school." Brown needed federal power to make it real.

sourceRef.quote: President Eisenhower responded by sending soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school.

encounters.prompt: At a sit-in, protesters sit where they're banned and refuse to leave. Three boxes describe the Greensboro sit-ins, and one is lying.

statements.text: On February 1, 1960, four students sat at a whites-only lunch counter
statements.explanation: It was the Woolworth counter in Greensboro.

statements.text: Nonviolent meant the students tried not to cause any conflict
statements.explanation: They broke the rules on purpose and stayed put. Staying calm took discipline.

statements.text: The sit-ins spread to more than 50 cities and led to a new student group, SNCC
statements.explanation: SNCC, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, formed in April 1960.

hints: Sitting at a counter where you're banned is already a challenge to the rules.
Nonviolent means you don't hit back when attacked. Test each box against students who broke a rule on purpose.
The box about February 1, 1960 is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That box is true. Look for the one that makes nonviolent sound like doing nothing.
encounters.debriefLine: The lying box said "Nonviolent meant the students tried not to cause any conflict." Nonviolent protest broke unfair rules on purpose and met violence with calm.

sourceRef.quote: On February 1, 1960, four Black college students sat down at a whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina.

encounters.targetMisconception: The federal government led the civil rights movement.
encounters.prompt: In 1961, Black and white Freedom Riders rode buses together to test a new ruling. Link each event to what it caused.

nodes: The Supreme Court bans segregated bus stations for travel between states
Black and white Freedom Riders ride buses into the Deep South to test the ruling
A mob firebombs a bus in Anniston, Alabama, and beats the riders
Photos of the burning bus appear in newspapers across the country
President Kennedy's team pushes the bus agency, the ICC, to enforce the ruling
decoys: Congress passes the Civil Rights Act

hints: The riders got on the buses to test something. Find the event they were testing.
Look for what turned the Anniston attack into news across the country. That link comes right after the attack.
Congress passed no civil rights law in 1961, so leave that one out. Kennedy's push comes last.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Follow the pressure. Washington only acted after the attack on the riders made national news.
encounters.debriefLine: The Freedom Rides were a chain. Riders tested a ruling, and their beating made headlines that pushed Washington to act.

sourceRef.quote: In Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses and beat the riders as they escaped.

encounters.prompt: Birmingham, Alabama, spring 1963. Link each event to the one it caused.

nodes: The SCLC, King's group, and local activists march against segregation in Birmingham
Bull Connor's police turn dogs and fire hoses on marchers, many of them children
TV and newspapers show the pictures across the country
Many Americans change their minds, and pressure on the White House grows
President Kennedy proposes a big civil rights bill, a plan for a new law, in June 1963
decoys: The Voting Rights Act bans literacy tests for voters

hints: Everything starts with the marches in Birmingham. Ask what happened to the marchers next.
The pictures only mattered once people saw them. Find what came after TV and the newspapers.
The Voting Rights Act card is from 1965, so leave it out. Kennedy's bill is the last link.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Kennedy's bill had causes behind it. Trace what people had to see before anyone in Washington acted.
encounters.debriefLine: In Birmingham, one thing led to the next. Kennedy only proposed his bill after the whole country saw the violence.

sourceRef.quote: The images shocked the nation, and in June 1963 President Kennedy proposed a sweeping civil rights bill.

encounters.targetMisconception: The march was only about King's speech.
encounters.prompt: In August 1963, about 250,000 people came to the March on Washington. Link each person to their part.

pairs.right: Longtime labor leader who first called for the march
pairs.why: He'd planned a march on Washington as far back as 1941.

pairs.right: Main organizer who planned how the day would run
pairs.why: He worked out how to move and guide the huge crowd.

pairs.right: Gave the last speech, known as 'I Have a Dream'
pairs.why: He spoke last, at the Lincoln Memorial.

pairs.right: Asked for jobs and freedom, including a federal jobs program
pairs.why: Its full name was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

decoyRights: Signed the Civil Rights Act into law

hints: The march's full name was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. One part matches those words.
Randolph and Rustin were both organizers. One had the idea years earlier, and one ran the day itself.
Nobody at the march signed the Civil Rights Act into law. A president did that the next year.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Labor and civil rights leaders organized this march around jobs too. King's speech closed the day.
encounters.debriefLine: You matched 4 people to their parts. The march was a planned demand for jobs and freedom, with King's speech at the end.

sourceRef.quote: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

encounters.targetMisconception: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 guaranteed the right to vote.
encounters.prompt: These cards come from two different laws. File each one under the law it belongs to.

bins.label: Civil Rights Act of 1964
bins.feature: fought segregation and unfair treatment in public places and jobs

bins.label: Voting Rights Act of 1965
bins.feature: protected the right to sign up and vote

items.text: Outlawed segregation in restaurants, hotels and theaters
items.why: Public places were Title II of the 1964 act.

items.text: Banned treating workers unfairly because of race, sex, religion or national origin
items.why: That's Title VII of the 1964 act.

items.text: Banned reading tests that kept people from signing up to vote
items.why: Ending these literacy tests was a main part of the 1965 act.

items.text: Sent federal officials to sign up voters where Black voters had been blocked
items.why: These officials were how the 1965 act was enforced.

items.text: Signed by Lyndon Johnson on July 2, 1964
items.why: That's the day the Civil Rights Act was signed.

items.text: Passed after the Selma marches of March 1965
items.why: Selma pushed the voting bill through Congress.

hints: Each card is about daily life and jobs, or about voting. That decides where it goes.
Try the card about restaurants and hotels. It's about public places, so ask which law covered those.
Two cards only give dates, July 1964 and March 1965. Match each to the year in a law's name.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The 1964 law fought segregation and unfair hiring. Voting protections came with the 1965 law.
encounters.debriefLine: You filed 6 cards under the right law. The 1964 act opened public places and jobs, and the 1965 act protected the vote.

sourceRef.quote: The act outlawed segregation in public accommodations such as restaurants and hotels and banned employment discrimination.

encounters.targetMisconception: Events happened in the order the textbook mentions them.
encounters.prompt: The textbook lists these out of order. Set the planks by their dates, and leave out the one from another story.

steps: President Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act, July 2, 1964
Marchers are attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, March 7, 1965
The march from Selma reaches the state capitol in Montgomery, March 25, 1965
President Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act, August 6, 1965
decoys: The Montgomery bus boycott ends, December 1956

hints: Go by the dates on the planks. The page order in the chapter doesn't count.
Start with the plank from 1964. The rest of this story happened in 1965.
The December 1956 plank is from the bus boycott, so leave it out. Then sort the two March planks by day.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Use the dates. The Civil Rights Act came in July 1964, and the Voting Rights Act came in August 1965.
encounters.debriefLine: You set 4 events by date. The attack on the Selma bridge, called Bloody Sunday, came between the two laws.

sourceRef.quote: On March 7, 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday.

encounters.prompt: A primary source was made at the time by someone who was there. File each document as primary or secondary.

bins.label: Primary source
bins.feature: made at the time by someone who took part or saw it

bins.label: Secondary source
bins.feature: made later by someone explaining what happened

items.text: A 1963 photo of marchers at the Lincoln Memorial
items.why: A witness took it at the march.

items.text: A 1971 textbook chapter about the civil rights movement
items.why: It's old, but the writer wasn't there. They wrote about it later.

items.text: The text of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
items.why: It's the law itself, from that time.
It explains the events decades later.

items.text: John Lewis's 1965 hospital interview about Bloody Sunday
items.why: He was there, and he spoke about it at the time.

items.text: A historian's 1988 book about King's life
items.why: Someone who studied the events wrote it later.

hints: Look at who made each document and when. How old it is doesn't decide it.
Test the 2019 film about Selma. Its makers weren't there, so they learned it from older sources.
The 1963 photo and the 1971 textbook are both old. Only one was made by someone at the march.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Age doesn't decide it. A 1971 textbook about 1963 is secondary, and a 1963 photo is primary.
encounters.debriefLine: You filed 6 documents by who made them and when. That's what makes a source primary or secondary.

sourceRef.quote: A primary source is created by a participant or witness at the time of the events, such as a letter, a photograph, or a speech.

encounters.targetMisconception: History is a list of unrelated events.
encounters.prompt: Link the events from Birmingham in 1963 to the Voting Rights Act in 1965. Two cards belong to an earlier story.

nodes: TV shows violence in Birmingham, and the country is shocked, May 1963
President Kennedy proposes a civil rights bill, June 1963
President Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act, July 1964
TV shows Bloody Sunday in Selma across the country, March 1965
Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act, August 1965
decoys: The Supreme Court decides Brown v. Board, 1954

hints: Start with the TV pictures from Birmingham in May 1963. End with the vote in August 1965.
Each new law came after the country saw violence on TV. Find the crisis before each law.
Brown in 1954 and Montgomery in 1955 are too early for this chain. Leave them out.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Each link is a cause and what it led to. Brown and Montgomery matter, but they're part of an earlier story.
encounters.debriefLine: Birmingham led to Kennedy's bill and the 1964 act. Then Selma led to the 1965 act.

sourceRef.quote: Again and again, televised violence against nonviolent protesters turned a local campaign into national legislation.

encounters.targetMisconception: History is a list of unrelated events.
encounters.prompt: The Editor asks why the Voting Rights Act passed in 1965, and not sooner. Use the clues to rule out explanations until one is left.

params.question: Why did Congress pass the Voting Rights Act in August 1965?

hypotheses.text: TV showed the violence at Selma in March 1965, and the pressure pushed Johnson to act within days
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had already fixed voting, so the 1965 law was just a small update
It was bound to happen after Brown in 1954, with or without anything else
The Supreme Court ordered Congress to pass it

clues.text: The 1964 act covered public places and jobs. In early 1965, fewer than 2% of Black adults in Selma's county were signed up to vote.
Johnson asked Congress for the voting bill on March 15, 1965, eight days after Bloody Sunday. He told them, 'We shall overcome.'
No court in 1965 told Congress to pass a law. The bill came from the White House.
From 1957 to 1964, three federal laws touched voting, but sign-ups barely moved. Eleven years after Brown, there was still no voting law.

hints: Start with the clue about the 2% of Black adults signed up to vote in early 1965.
If under 2% could vote after the 1964 act, that act hadn't fixed voting. Strike that explanation.
The court clue rules out one more. Then test the explanation about Brown against the March 15, 1965 clue.
encounters.wrongFeedback: One of your clues rules that one out. Find the clue that says it can't be true.
encounters.debriefLine: You ruled out three explanations with dated clues. The Voting Rights Act came fast after TV showed the violence at Selma.

sourceRef.quote: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned literacy tests and sent federal registrars to counties that had blocked Black voters.

intro.text: The files run from 1954 to 1965. Walk the years in order and put the true story back.

outro.text: That's the story. People pushed for years, and that's how the laws passed.

beats.text: This chapter tells things out of order. Go by the dates.
Here's my question. Why did the voting law pass in 1965?

pre.prompt: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do?
Which is a primary source about the 1963 March on Washington?
choices: A photograph taken at the march

post.prompt: Which of these was NOT part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
choices: Outlawing segregation in hotels and restaurants
Banning literacy tests, the reading tests for voters

post.prompt: What kind of source is a 1975 textbook chapter about the 1963 March on Washington?
choices: Secondary, because it explains the events later
Primary, because it's about a real event
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was signed
The Voting Rights Act was signed
The Selma march reached the state capitol
